opus-5.5.text:
I think it was one of the hardest decisions we've made, but in hindsight, I believe it was the right one.

Taichi started as my research project at MIT. The goal was to make high-performance computer graphics and simulation programming much easier, so researchers and engineers could write a few lines of Python and get GPU-level performance. I'm still very proud of it. It has a wonderful open-source community, and many people in academia and industry use it.

But when you run a company, you have to be honest with yourself about one question: are you creating enough value that people will pay for it, and can that support a team long-term? With a programming language or a compiler, the value is real but very indirect. Developers love free tools, and the people who benefit most are often several steps away from whoever would sign a contract. We tried different approaches, and it was hard to find a business model that scaled.

At the same time, generative AI was changing very quickly. Around 2023 we saw that 3D content creation was a huge bottleneck. Games, film, e-commerce, VR, and robotics simulation all need 3D assets. Making a good 3D model by hand can take an artist days or weeks. With AI, that could become seconds or minutes. That's a much more direct kind of value. You can see it right away: you type a prompt or upload an image, and you get a usable mesh.

So the shift to Meshy wasn't really abandoning what we did before. It was more like moving up the stack. Our team's background is in graphics, geometry, rendering, and high-performance computing, and all of that is extremely relevant to generating good 3D assets. The Taichi experience taught us how to build infrastructure and how to care about performance and quality. Meshy lets us apply that to a problem where users feel the benefit immediately.

There was definitely some emotional difficulty. When you've spent years on something, it feels like your child. Some people in the community worried we would stop caring about Taichi. But I think a startup's first responsibility is to survive and create real value. If you can't do that, you can't support anything else, including open source.

Looking back, I would say: be loyal to the problem and to your users, not to a particular piece of technology. Technology is a means. For us, the underlying mission has always been to make 3D creation accessible to more people. Taichi was one way to approach that, and Meshy is a more direct way.

r001.rationale: The response says the company noticed a 3D-content bottleneck and saw generative AI as an opportunity, but it does not state that seeing Taichi used to implement 3D techniques prompted exploration of 3D-asset generation.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it was one of the hardest decisions I've ever made, and also one I'm quite at peace with now.

Taichi started as my PhD project at MIT. The idea was simple: make it easy for people to write high-performance physics simulation and graphics code in Python, and let the compiler handle the hard parts. We open-sourced it, built a community of tens of thousands of developers, and I'm genuinely proud of that. People used Taichi for fluid simulation, soft-body physics, autonomous driving simulation, teaching, all sorts of things.

But a compiler infrastructure project and a company are two different animals. We spent years trying to figure out how a general-purpose programming language becomes a sustainable business. We tried cloud services, enterprise support, consulting-style engagements. The problem was that our users loved the tool, but the people who paid for it were scattered across completely different industries with completely different needs. Each deal required custom work. We couldn't find that repeatable wedge where one product solves one painful problem for a well-defined group of customers.

So around the time generative AI started to really take off, we asked ourselves a tough question: what do we actually know how to do better than almost anyone? The answer was graphics and geometry, the deep stuff, meshes, materials, rendering, the pipeline between a mathematical representation and something that looks good on screen. And when we looked at 3D content creation, we saw a market that was clearly broken. Making a production-quality 3D asset still takes a skilled artist hours or days. Game studios, e-commerce, film, XR, all of them are starved for 3D content. And the AI models that generate 3D were producing blobs that looked fine in a demo but were useless in a real pipeline, bad topology, no UVs, no clean materials.

That's where Meshy came from. Instead of building a tool for programmers, we're building a tool for creators, and we're using everything we learned from Taichi, the GPU infrastructure, the geometry processing, the obsession with performance, to make generated assets actually usable in production.

I won't pretend the transition was painless. We had to tell a passionate open-source community that the company's focus was moving. Some people were upset, and I understand that. Taichi still exists and is still open source, and I'm happy for the community to carry it forward. But I think a founder's job is to be honest about what the market is telling you, not to protect your own past work out of pride.

What surprised me is how much faster everything moved once we had a clear user. With Taichi, we'd ship a feature and wait months to see if anyone cared. With Meshy, millions of people are generating assets, and the feedback loop is daily. That energy is addictive. So, in hindsight, I view the shift less as abandoning Taichi and more as finally finding the problem that all of that technology was meant to solve.

astra-6.text:
I see it as a shift in focus, from building a general-purpose technology to solving a concrete problem for users. With Taichi, the starting point is the technology: what can we make possible? With Mesh and 3D assets, the starting point is the user: what do they want to create, and what’s stopping them?

Of course, that means changing how we think. Technical sophistication alone isn’t enough. The output has to be useful, and the experience has to fit into someone’s workflow. A powerful system that people struggle to use isn’t yet a good product.

So I wouldn’t judge the decision just by whether we stayed with the original direction. I’d judge it by whether we can turn our technical strengths into something people actually want to use. That’s the opportunity—and the challenge—in making this shift.

sol-6.1.text:
I see it as a shift in how we apply our technology. With Taichi, we were focused on giving developers a tool for building things. Moving toward Mesh and 3D assets brings us closer to the result people actually want: something they can use in their creative work.

That also changes the questions we have to ask. Technical performance matters, but so do the quality of the asset, how easily someone can edit it, and whether it fits into their workflow. It’s a substantial change in product focus, while still building on our interest in graphics and making creation more accessible.
